sources: Penn State Extension, Brown Marmorated Stink Bug: accidentally introduced from East Asia, first collected in Allentown, PA in 1998; adults seek sheltered places such as houses in fall; scent glands release defensive chemicals that can be an aeroallergen; crushing on skin can cause dermatitis in a small percentage of people; does not reproduce in or damage structures; feeds on apples (cat-facing makes fruit unmarketable), peaches, tomatoes, corn and more; adults about 17 mm, nearly as wide as long, banded antennae; vacuuming works but the vacuum may keep the smell; seal entry points with caulk; https://extension.psu.edu/brown-marmorated-stink-bug

Inkley 2012, Journal of Entomological Science 47(2): 125-130, Characteristics of home invasion by the brown marmorated stink bug: 26,205 adults collected inside one home in Washington County, Maryland over a 181-day study (January-June 2011); blocking exits from walls into living space reduced the collection rate but did not halt it; https://doi.org/10.18474/0749-8004-47.2.125

beats.say: Thousands of stink bugs are crawling out of your walls.
One man in Maryland caught over twenty six thousand inside his house, in six months.
The brown marmorated stink bug. Shaped like a shield, with striped antennae.
In the fall, they crawl into your house, to spend the winter.
Squeeze one, and glands on its body let out a stinking spray.
They don't breed in your house, and they don't damage it.
So don't crush them. Even your vacuum will stink for a while.
